items.prompt: A newly enrolled student has no graded or missing submissions. What does calculateSectionGrade report, and what is the downside?
items.answer: 100% 'Excellent', so new students show Low risk and are invisible to the risk system
distractors: 0% 'Failing', which floods the dashboard with false critical-risk alerts for every newly enrolled student
NaN, because it divides zero earned points by zero possible points and the badge renders 'NaN%'
null, and every page hides the grade badge for that student
items.explanation: When totalPointsPossible <= 0 the rule returns percentage 100. The guide calls it a deliberate 'innocent until proven guilty' product decision with a real downside; 04 says it is now pinned by a characterisation test.

items.prompt: A student has one Graded submission (8 of 10) and one Submitted-but-ungraded submission worth 10. What percentage does calculateSectionGrade return?
items.answer: 80%: ungraded work is added then subtracted, so only graded work counts
distractors: 40%: the ungraded submission counts as 0 out of 10 until a teacher grades it
90%: the ungraded submission is treated as full marks until it is graded, to avoid penalizing the student
100%: any ungraded item makes the rule fall back to the no-graded-work default
items.explanation: Line 43 adds pointsPossible for every submission, and the else branch subtracts it for statuses other than Graded, Returned or Missing; the net effect excludes Submitted work from the denominator.

items.prompt: A student is failing one class and acing three others. What does their 'Section Average' risk badge show today?
items.answer: A healthy average, because risk badges still pool submissions from all of the student's sections; only the gradebook is scoped per section
distractors: The failing class's grade, because the badge shows the student's worst section
Four separate badges, one per section
An error, because the risk badge requires exactly one section
items.explanation: B3 still stands for risk badges: the student page feeds every submission of the student (all sections) into calculateSectionGrade and then calculateStudentRisk, so one failing class can be averaged away. Story 7's gradebook is correctly scoped.

items.prompt: Two workers try to run the same Queued job at once. Why does claimJob use updateMany with a status filter instead of reading the row and then calling update?
items.answer: The status check lives in the write's WHERE, so the database picks one winner (count 1 vs 0)
distractors: updateMany is faster than update on SQLite, so the window between the two workers becomes too small to matter
update cannot increment a column atomically, so the attempts counter could not be maintained with it
updateMany locks the whole table until the job finishes running
items.explanation: SELECT-then-UPDATE lets both workers see Queued and both execute. updateMany({ where: { id, status: { in: RUNNABLE } } }) returns a count, and only one call can match.

items.prompt: After Story 3, how can a DeadLettered job run again?
items.answer: Only via an explicit requeue to Queued, which resets the attempt budget
distractors: By clicking Retry Now on the jobs page, which runs it immediately exactly as it did before Story 3
Automatically, once processQueue sees that attempts is still below maxAttempts for that job
Never: DeadLettered has no outgoing transitions at all
items.explanation: JOB_TRANSITIONS maps DeadLettered to ['Queued'] only, and canRunJob accepts only Queued, Failed and Retrying, so the UI and worker now share one predicate.

items.prompt: Why does buildStudentScope return a Prisma WHERE fragment instead of filtering fetched students in JavaScript?
items.answer: A post-fetch filter breaks once someone adds take, count or an aggregate over unfiltered rows
distractors: Prisma cannot return students whose relations have not been loaded, so filtering in JavaScript would crash
JavaScript filters run on the client and cannot read the session cookie that identifies the viewer
WHERE fragments are cached by Next.js between requests, so pages render faster
items.explanation: Pushing the constraint into the query means it cannot be forgotten downstream; the scope module explains the 'silently too high' total leak of filtering after fetching.

items.prompt: A user row has a role string that buildStudentScope does not recognize. Which students can they see?
items.answer: None: the default branch returns { id: '__no_access__' }, failing closed
distractors: All students, like Admin, because an empty object is returned
Only students in their own sections, like a Teacher
The request throws, because the switch has no default branch
items.explanation: Role is a plain string column, so an unknown value is possible; the default case matches no real id, which is the only safe default.

items.prompt: A student who was dropped from a section tries to enrol in it again. What happens, and why?
items.answer: Rejected as 'already enrolled': the Dropped row still exists and findUnique counts it
distractors: It succeeds, because dropStudentAction deleted the enrollment row when the student was dropped
It succeeds and creates a second Enrollment row with status Enrolled next to the Dropped one
It is placed on the waitlist automatically
items.explanation: @@unique([studentId, classSectionId]) plus a status-only drop means a second row is impossible; hasExistingEnrollment is !!existing from findUnique. 04 notes this is now load-bearing for waitlist promotion.

items.prompt: recordAttendanceAction is saving a 30-student register and the database errors on student 17. What is left behind?
items.answer: A half-recorded register: students 1-16 are saved, the rest are not
distractors: Nothing: the loop runs inside db.$transaction, so all 16 earlier upserts roll back with the failure
All 30 rows, because upsert retries failed writes
Only the audit rows, because the audit write happens before each upsert in the loop
items.explanation: The loop does a findUnique, an upsert and an audit write per student, each its own statement; 04 confirms there is still no $transaction anywhere.

items.prompt: One caller records attendance for '2026-05-22' and another for '2026-05-22T09:00:00Z'. What happens on the unique key [studentId, classSectionId, date]?
items.answer: Two rows for the same day: the bare date becomes midnight UTC, the timestamped one a different DateTime, so the upsert does not match
distractors: One row, because the date schema strips the time component
One row, because Prisma compares DateTime values by calendar day
The second call is rejected by zod as an invalid date
items.explanation: The input schema only checks that new Date(v) parses, and the action does new Date(date). Idempotency holds only while every writer sends a bare YYYY-MM-DD string.

items.prompt: Story 13 centralised UI gating and Story 15 scoped reads. What is still the top remaining security item?
items.answer: Server Actions still trust the given actorId and never re-check permissions
distractors: Pages still gate actions with inline role arrays instead of the central permission table
Any role can still open any student's profile, because scoping was only added to the list pages
Passwords are stored in plain text in the seed
items.explanation: C1 is only partially addressed: recordAttendanceAction, for example, takes actorId in its payload and parses its shape, but nothing checks that the caller may record attendance.

items.prompt: In the support-notes filter, the AdminOnly line needs the cast (activeUser.role as string) === 'Admin'. What does that cast reveal?
items.answer: The branch is unreachable: an earlier line already returned true for Admin, so TypeScript narrowed 'Admin' out, and SchoolManager sees AdminOnly notes through that same earlier line
distractors: role is typed any, so comparisons need a cast to compile
The cast is required because Admin is stored in lowercase in the database
The cast makes AdminOnly notes visible to Advisors as well
items.explanation: The early return grants Admin and SchoolManager everything before the AdminOnly check; gotcha C5 names this as both a leak to SchoolManager and an unreachable branch.

items.front: getActiveUser falls back to the 'admin' user when the cookie is missing or points at a deleted user. Risk?
items.back: Fail-open authentication: no session means full admin rights. Acceptable only for this lab's dev switcher; a real deployment must reject the request (401) instead.

items.front: How do you claim a queue row safely with Prisma?
items.back: updateMany({ where: { id, status: { in: RUNNABLE } }, data: { status: 'Running', attempts: { increment: 1 } } }) and treat count === 1 as the claim. The guard must be part of the write condition, not a prior SELECT.

items.front: The repo shipped a 15-table dev.db against a 17-table schema and tsc, next build and 129 tests all passed. Lessons?
items.back: A generated artefact in version control is a liability (dev.db is now gitignored and rebuilt by db:push + db:seed), and a green build is not a running application: start the process, because only that read the real database.

items.front: Permission check vs data scope: what question does each answer?
items.back: Permission (canPerformAction): may this role do the action at all, e.g. grade? Scope (buildStudentScope): whose data, e.g. which students' work? A Teacher may grade, but only students in sections they teach.
